title: Who Really Invented the Croissant? (It's Not Who You Think)

segments.text: Picture breakfast in Paris. A cup of coffee, and next to it, the most French thing on the table: a croissant.
Golden, glossy, and so flaky it leaves evidence all over your shirt.
Here's the twist. For most of its history, this pastry wasn't French. And it wasn't flaky, either.
Its story starts in another city, under a different name, and it comes wrapped in one of the most famous food legends in Europe. A legend that historians say doesn't hold up.
So where did the croissant really come from? Let's follow the crescent.
Our first stop is Vienna, Austria, and a bread roll called the kipfel.
A kipfel is a small roll shaped like a crescent moon. You'll also see it spelled kipferl, and Austria still lists it as a traditional food today.
How old is it? Old. Vienna's city historians point to a medieval chronicle that describes the city's bakers presenting crescent rolls to Duke Leopold at Christmas, in the year 1227.
We should be careful here. A chronicle isn't a receipt, and nobody wrote down the recipe. We don't know exactly what that roll tasted like.
But the name keeps turning up. Austria's food heritage register lists mentions of kipfel in Vienna in 1630, 1652, and 1670.
Some researchers think it may have started as a monastery bread baked for Easter. That part is a guess, and the source says so.
What matters for our story is the timeline. By the late 1600s, the crescent roll had already been part of Viennese life for a very long time.
And that kipfel was bread. Shaped by hand and baked as a roll. No butter layers. No shattering crust.
Now for the legend. If you've ever looked up the croissant, you've read it.
The year is 1683. The army of the Ottoman Empire has surrounded Vienna, and the siege drags on for weeks.
According to the story, the attackers try to tunnel under the city walls at night. And who's awake in the middle of the night? Bakers.
The bakers hear the digging and raise the alarm, and the city is saved. To celebrate, they bake a roll shaped like the crescent on the enemy's flags.
It's a wonderful story. It has danger, heroes, and breakfast.
It also has problems. No account from the time has been found that mentions it. Vienna's own city history calls the tale, quote, historically untenable.
And remember our timeline. The kipfel was already in Viennese records decades before the siege, and in that old chronicle, centuries before.
There's even a second version of the same legend, set three years later in Budapest. When one story happens in two cities, that's usually a sign it's a story.
Vienna's city history even names the writer who did the most to spread the tale: an author named Moritz Bermann.
Legend number two stars Marie Antoinette. Born in Vienna and married into the French royal family in 1770, she supposedly missed her kipfel so much that she had it baked in France.
Charming. But food historians call that one a myth, too, and Austria's own heritage register only says she allegedly did it.
So if it wasn't a siege, and it wasn't a queen, how did a Viennese bread roll end up in Paris? The best documented answer is a man with a business plan.
His name was August Zang. He was born in Vienna in 1807, and he had served as an artillery officer in the Austrian army.
Around 1838 or 1839, and the accounts don't quite agree on the year, Zang opened a bakery in Paris. It was called the Boulangerie Viennoise: the Viennese Bakery.
His bakers made the breads of home, including the kipfel and a crusty roll called the Kaisersemmel.
Paris noticed. By late 1839, a French writer was already mentioning the Viennese bakery in a letter to a friend.
An American magazine later reported that Zang did, quote, an excellent business with his Viennese rolls.
And success attracts imitators. French bakers opened their own Viennese bakeries and made their own version of the little crescent.
They gave it a French name that simply describes its shape. Croissant means crescent.
By 1863, the word had made it into a major French dictionary, defined as a small bread or cake in the shape of a crescent.
And Viennese baking kept its shine in Paris. According to Austria's food heritage register, the Viennese bakery was a big hit at the Paris World's Fair of 1867.
Zang himself didn't stay to watch. In 1848 he went home to Vienna and founded a newspaper, Die Presse. Its first issue came out that July.
He made his name in publishing, not pastry. The man who brought the crescent to Paris went down in history as a newspaper man.
But here's the thing. The croissant he left behind still wasn't the croissant you know.
For decades, the French croissant was basically a crescent-shaped bread roll. Soft, pleasant, and not flaky at all.
The transformation came when French bakers combined that shape with a technique from their own pastry kitchens: lamination.
Exactly when is debated. One account puts the shift near the end of the 1800s. The recipes most often cited were printed a few years later, around 1905 and 1906.
French bakers call the result pâte levée feuilletée. In plain English: leavened, layered dough.
Here's how it works. You start with a yeast dough, like bread. Then you wrap it around a flat slab of cold butter.
Roll it out long, and fold it in thirds, like a letter. That one sheet of butter is now three.
Chill it, roll it, fold it again. Nine layers. Once more: twenty-seven.
Bakers vary the number of folds, but the idea is always the same: dozens of paper-thin sheets of butter, each one separated by dough.
Then the dough is rolled thin and cut into long triangles, and each triangle is rolled up from the wide end to the point. That's what gives a croissant its stepped, spiraled back.
Now the oven takes over. The water in the dough turns to steam. The steam pushes the layers apart, and they set into a crisp, open crumb.
Cut one open and you can see it: a web of air pockets, wrapped in a crust that shatters when you bite it.
That's the real difference between the two cousins. The kipfel is bread. The croissant is bread that learned a pastry trick.
It's also why the croissant belongs to a family the French call viennoiserie. The name still remembers where the idea came from.
All that folding takes time, skill, and a cool kitchen. Which is exactly the kind of work that factories love to take over.
In the 1970s, manufacturers worked out how to make croissants by machine and freeze them before baking.
Suddenly a shop didn't need a trained baker. It needed a freezer and an oven. In France, a chain called La Croissanterie opened its first shop in 1977.
America took the idea and ran with it. In 1983, Burger King put a breakfast sandwich on a croissant and called it the Croissan'wich.
The croissant had gone from a Viennese specialty in Paris to a fast food bun in under a hundred and fifty years.
Even in France, many bakery croissants now start as factory-made frozen dough. Estimates of how many vary widely, and people argue about the number.
One food historian takes it calmly. As he puts it, most things that are meticulous about a croissant can be industrialized.
So, is the croissant French?
The shape is Viennese, and very old. The name is French, from the 1800s. The flaky layers are French too, and surprisingly recent.

The siege and the queen make better stories. But the documented version is pretty good on its own: a soldier turned baker, a busy shop in Paris, and generations of bakers who kept folding butter into dough.
So the next time one falls apart all over your plate, you'll know. Those crumbs took more than six hundred years to make.
